name: Currarino syndrome (sacral agenesis + anorectal + presacral mass)

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: Defined by a triad of a sacral bony defect, an anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass
The characteristic sacral anomaly is a hemisacrum with a crescentic (scimitar) sacral defect that spares the first sacral segment
The anorectal component ranges from anal stenosis and chronic constipation to a frank anorectal malformation
The presacral mass is most often an anterior meningocele, a teratoma, an enteric duplication cyst, or a combination of these
Frequently familial with autosomal dominant inheritance linked to MNX1 (HLXB9) mutations, so family screening is worthwhile
Chronic refractory constipation from birth, especially with a sacral abnormality on radiograph, should prompt evaluation for the triad
Management is individualised, addressing the anorectal defect surgically and resecting or repairing the presacral mass with neurosurgical input for a meningocele
reference.pathophysiology: Currarino syndrome is a developmental disorder of the caudal cell mass and notochord, in which abnormal separation of the neuroectoderm and endoderm and defective sacral formation produce the characteristic combination of anomalies. Many cases carry mutations in the MNX1 (HLXB9) homeobox gene, which is important in caudal and hindgut development. The resulting hemisacrum leaves a persistent anterior sacral defect through which a presacral mass such as an anterior meningocele, teratoma, or enteric duplication protrudes, while concurrent maldevelopment of the hindgut yields the anorectal malformation or anal stenosis. Tethered cord and other spinal dysraphic features may coexist.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated anorectal malformation without sacral or presacral anomaly
Hirschsprung disease as a cause of chronic constipation
additionalInvestigations: Sacral and pelvic radiographs to demonstrate the scimitar hemisacrum
Pelvic and spinal MRI to characterise the presacral mass and detect tethered cord or meningocele
Ultrasound of the spine and pelvis in the neonate
MNX1 (HLXB9) genetic testing and screening of first-degree relatives
Contrast studies or examination to define the anorectal anatomy
Assessment for associated urogenital and spinal anomalies
redFlags: Meningitis or signs of central nervous system infection from a communicating anterior meningocele
Neurological deterioration suggesting tethered cord or cord compression
Features raising concern for malignant change within a presacral teratoma
Severe obstructive symptoms from a large presacral mass
Recurrent urinary or faecal complications from the associated malformations
reference.prognosis: With recognition of all three components and appropriate surgical and neurosurgical management, prognosis is generally good, though continence outcomes depend on the anorectal lesion and sacral integrity. Undiagnosed meningocele risks life-threatening meningitis, and a small proportion of presacral teratomas may undergo malignant transformation.
pitfalls: Treating chronic constipation without imaging the sacrum and missing the underlying triad
Overlooking an anterior meningocele and risking meningitis during transrectal or perineal procedures
Assuming a presacral mass is benign without appropriate imaging and follow-up
Failing to screen family members despite autosomal dominant inheritance
Neglecting spinal cord tethering when planning management
